semanticRelations.rationale: Identical lexeme family does not imply the same referent in negated and first-person divine contexts.
A named place and a named altar must remain distinct types of commemorative naming.
Human use of ego eimi limits inference from the grammatical phrase alone; possible Johannine intertext requires contextual argument.
Explicit naming in Exodus does not itself reconstruct the sound of ancient YHWH pronunciation.
Greek Κυρίου at James 5:4 is genitive whereas κύριος at Romans 9:29 is nominative; the shared Σαβαὼθ does not erase differences of case and discourse.
The broader three-passage observation is narrowed to the Galatians 4:6 account of the Spirit crying; editorial grammar still requires independent review.

God is the referent of the self-identifying first-person formula; Moses is addressed. Comparison with John 8:58 must keep the referent, addressee, printed Greek wording and possible intertext distinct.

One identical MT expression belongs to the royal figure in Jer23:6 and the feminine city Jerusalem in Jer33:16. The latter's Old Greek status is a separate secondary research question, not the basis for confusing the Hebrew referents.
Both Hebrew loci name a city in their respective narrative contexts; this does not convert either expression into a stand-alone, verbatim divine personal self-naming.
Positive Rock metaphors referring to YHWH do not imply the two Rock expressions in Deut32:31 share a referent or are divine proper names.
Deut32:31 contains two opposed Rock referents, Deut32:37 rhetorically challenges non-YHWH gods; poetic pronoun changes and 32:30 are separately reviewed.
MT child's naming in Hebrew and Rahlfs-Hanhart printed καλέσεις are different textual editions with morphology that must be investigated, not silently made verbatim identical.
Rahlfs-Hanhart LXX Isaiah 7:14 καλέσεις (2 singular) and SBLGNT Matthew 1:23 καλέσουσιν (3 plural) differ as printed; textual/authorial explanation is open.
Isa 8:8 vocative/name allusion remains contextually contested, whereas Isa 8:10 is an explicit assurance clause; identical consonants do not make both child namings.
Matthew's christological citation and gloss of Isaiah are canonical reception, while precise historical Hebrew antecedent and original naming-verb forms need separate historical/critical evidence.
Same verse identifies Lord God in 1:8; narrator identifies throne speaker in 21:5. This distinguishes evidence, not necessarily persons.
21:6 is tied to throne speaker in v5; 22:13 is contextually linked to Jesus, named at 22:16; the evidence types differ.
Shared Alpha/Omega title does not erase explicit Lord God speech cue in 1:8 versus contextual inference in 22:13.
TR1550 longer 1:8 cannot silently rewrite the attested SBLGNT 1:8 verse.
Same plural-shaped lexeme can designate the creator YHWH or other gods depending on verb agreement and discourse; no morphological shortcut.
YHWH in Ex34:6 and Deut32:4 versus a foreign god whose presence is explicitly denied in Deut32:12.
Gideon names a new YHWH-shalom altar in 6:24 and is instructed to destroy his father's Baal altar in 6:25. Distinct cult objects.
Gen35:7 explicitly names a place, Jud6:24 explicitly names an altar; do not force a single naming type based on sacred vocabulary.
Ex15:26 YHWH addresses Israel, Jer17:14 Jeremiah requests healing FROM YHWH. Root identity does not turn prayer into divine first-person speech.
רֹפְאֶךָ has the second-person masculine singular suffix; מְקַדִּשְׁכֶם has second-person masculine plural. Context and addressee cannot be flattened.
Thematic canonical connection does not prove Hebrew and Greek are the same original-language clause, nor does it erase the difference between psalmist and Jesus as speaker.
The same formula in a fearful disciple scene and in an arrest identity-answer scene is not one speech act or automatically the same theological allusion.
The narrator in 18:6 cites the utterance of 18:5 when relating the party's fall; this cannot be counted as a second independent 'I am' statement.
John18:6 narrates and reports the earlier quote; John18:8 quotes Jesus directly, adding his protection request.
The previously blind man uses the same self-identification wording in John9:9; Jesus is speaker in John18:5, so wording alone cannot establish a divine lexeme.
John6:20 contains a short identity/assurance clause; the Greek Ex3:14 full wording and John8:58 intertext need independent investigation, not automatic equivalence.
Gen22:8 is Abraham's answer to Isaac without object naming; the named object in Gen22:14 is explicitly the place, not the altar.
Gen22:14 active Qal יִרְאֶה in place-name and Niphal יֵרָאֶה in subsequent communal mountain saying must remain distinct printed forms.
Moses' 17:15 naming of an altar is distinct from the difficult explanatory clause in 17:16; proposed נֵס is not the written MT כֵּס.
Printed MT wording in hand/throne/Yah differs from printed LXX secret-hand explanation; this does not independently establish a distinct ancient Vorlage.
Two direct divine identification speeches differ from Isaac's human blessing.
The retrospect in Ex6:3 alongside Genesis first-person forms does not resolve historical revelation or the contested name-knowledge issue by fiat.
Third-person Shiloh worship narration differs from David addressing Goliath.
David's battle invocation differs from the seraphim's heavenly holiness hymn.
Seraphim call one another versus Zechariah's first/third-person prophetic speech contexts.
Romans 9:29 quotes Isaiah 1:9, not the seraphim hymn Isaiah 6:3; a common divine title does not prove direct quotation of Isa6.
Genesis14:18 narrator reports Melchizedek as priest; 14:19–20 Melchizedek speaks blessing and doxology; do not treat narration as an utterance.
Melchizedek's blessing/doxology differs from Abram's oath to the king of Sodom with YHWH explicitly in the MT.
Abram's oath joins YHWH+El Elyon in printed MT, but that does not independently settle ancient historical identity of Melchizedek's cult or prove/disprove Cargill's attributed gloss hypothesis.
Ex34:14 gives explicit name/character clause inside divine speech; Deut4:24 is Moses' covenantal description with no name clause.
Exodus 34:14 distinguishes another worshiped god (לְאֵל אַחֵר) from YHWH, whose name/character is jealous; generic el cannot always be treated as divine YHWH designation.
Ancient of Days is the enthroned recipient of approach by a distinct 'like a son of man' visionary figure; theological later reception not identical to grammar.
Ancient of Days in v13 is approached; in v22 arrives and judgment benefits the saints. Shared title does not create a single scene/action nor fix later Christological reception.
Rev1:4 John's greeting contains sources introduced by ἀπὸ; Rev1:8 has the explicit quote attribution λέγει κύριος, ὁ θεός.
Rev1:8 God is directly named speaker whereas Rev21:22 John narrates a temple vision, with Lord God Almighty alongside Lamb.
Rev21:5–6 direct speech of throne-sitter introduced by narrator versus Rev21:22 John narrating the city's absent temple.

Daniel's Ancient and an approaching son-of-man-like figure, and Revelation's Lord God/Lamb coordinated as temple, are literary scenes with distinct lexemes; cross-testament Christology requires separate evidence, not automatic lexical identity.
Moses' two prayer addresses to YHWH differ from Isaiah's reporting seeing Adonai as an object, not two direct divine utterances.
Psalm8 אֲדֹנֵינוּ with communal first-person suffix is not vocalized אֲדֹנָי in Exodus34 nor the human honorific אֲדֹנִי in Genesis23.
Isaiah1 prophetic indictment names Holy One as rejected object; Isaiah43 YHWH gives first-person identification as Israel's God and Savior.
Isa43 divine self-declaration differs from Isa47 poetically placed plural-community Redeemer intervention with literary voice requiring review.
Isa47 community/narrative Redeemer YHWH Sabaoth line cannot be recast as the angelic Isa6 holiness hymn simply because YHWH of hosts appears in both.
Ex15 song records a free Yah while Ps68:5 MT records prefixed bet Yah; NET suggested ki substitution is not the printed Hebrew line.
Yah is a shortened biblical name designation associated with YHWH; the common divine referent does not make an unrelated deity or settle the historical vocalization of the full tetragrammaton.
